## Limits
The idea of a limit is what value does a function approach when the input approaches a discontinuous point on the graph.
$\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$

The values of f(x) approach L as x approaches c.
So c is a real number that x cannot be since it is discontinuous.
L is the value that x would approximately be if it was at c. (the number its approaching)

The limit of f(x) does not equal f(x). The solution to a limit is a point where the function is undefined or discontinuous. We want to know where it is discontinuous, not its actual value.

NOTE: For jump discontinuities, the limit exists at where the hole is, not where the actual value is.
NOTE: The limit of a function does not exist if the value of L as x approaches c is different if you approach from the left or right. It should be the same regardless of what direction you approach it from.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Most of them basically mean that if you have a limit + something that is not a limit, just take the limit of that something and you can do the operation.
The limits of a constant function is always k
The limit of x is x = c
Useful to remember that x^exp is just x * x * x * whatever. Or just take a shortcut and say x^anything is just c^anything (shortcut only works if the x term is by itself)

Use the properties to simplify as best you can and you can get numbers out of x's without solving.

Left side limits are written as c^-1 if the values of f(x) approach L as x approaches c from the left, that is, x approaches c and x < c
Right side limits are written as c+ if the values of f(x) approach L as x approaches c from the right, that is, x approaches c and x > c
*The limit of f(x) exists if and only if the two side limits are equal.*

If f(x) gets as close to a number L as we please when x gets sufficiently large, then we write lim(x -> infinity) f(x) = L
It can also approach negative infinity
Typically when you have an asymptote.

The function f is continuous at x = c if f is defined at x = c and if:
Lim(x -> c) = f(c) or it has to exist
f(x) is as close as we want to f(c) provided x is close enough to c. The function is continuous on an interval [a, b] if it is continuous at every point in the interval.

Continuous functions that are continuous at any point in their domain are:
- Linear functions
- Polynomials
- Exponential function
- Logarithms
- Trigonometric functions

## Continuity of Sums, Products, and Quotients of Functions

Suppose that f and g are continuous on an interval. Then, on that same interval:
- If b is a constant, then bf(x) is continuous
- f(x) + g(x) is continuous (or subtraction)
- f(x)g(x) is continuous
- f(x) / g(x) is continuous, provided g(x) != 0 on the interval

What is not on that list is composite. If f and g are continuous, and if the composite function f(g(x)) is defined on an interval, then f(g(x)) is continuous on that interval.
Ln functions are continuous over their domain, which starts as lnx [1, infinity] but can be different. (maybe)

## Velocity
*Velocity* is the distance travelled by an object in a unit of time.
To compute velocity we need to know how the position of the object changes in time. This is given by a function:
s(t) = position of the object at time t.

If s(t) is the position of an object at time t, then the average velocity of the object over the interval a <= t <= b is:
AV = change in position/change in time = $\frac{s(b)-s(a)}{b - a}$

![](data:image/png;base64,)

In words, the average velocity of an object over an interval is the change in position during the interval divided by the change in time. The unit for velocity is the unit of distance (the nominator) divided by the units of time (denominator).
It can be viewed geometrically as the slope between the points (a, s(a)) and (b, s(b)) on the graph y = s(t). This line is also known as the secant line
M = (s(b) - s(a)) / (b - a)   <--- just the slope formula

The *instantaneous velocity* at t = a is defined as:
$\lim_{h\to0} \left(\frac{s(a+h)-s(a)}{h}\right)$

It's basically making the interval of average velocity so small that you're approximating the velocity at a specific point.

It does not have a secant line, it has a tangent line. It only meets the graph of the function at ONE POINT, which is the instantaneous velocity at t = c. It is the slope of the line tangent to the graph y = s(t) at point (c, s(c)).

Velocity is a *signed* quantity, it can be positive or negative depending on the direction it is moving.
Speed is the *magnitude of velocity* and doesn't take direction into account. It is always positive.
